_meta.purpose: Layer-1 case index for semantic retrieval (Option A). One rich record per case. Feed the whole array (cached) to Claude alongside a user's project description; Claude returns the most relevant cases + winning arguments.

provenance_legend.public_record: Populated from public court records and Claude's knowledge of these landmark cases. NOT yet verified line-by-line against the folder PDFs.
provenance_legend.doc_verified: Checked against the opinions/expert reports in the case folder.

_meta.caveat: All records are provenance='public_record'. Verify outcome, expert names, winning_arguments, judge_treatment, citation pinpoints, and citation.stands_for dispositions against the folder PDFs before customer-facing use. Where a reporter page was uncertain, citation.cite gives docket + court + date (always safe).

economic_models_vocabulary.market_definition_demand_substitution: Relevant-market proof via demand substitution / hypothetical monopolist.
economic_models_vocabulary.unilateral_effects_diversion: Post-merger unilateral price effects from diversion between close competitors.
economic_models_vocabulary.coordinated_effects: Increased risk of tacit/express coordination post-merger.
economic_models_vocabulary.maverick_disruptor_loss: Loss of a maverick / low-price disruptor's competitive constraint.
economic_models_vocabulary.merger_simulation: Structural simulation of post-merger prices (demand system).
economic_models_vocabulary.upp_guppi: Upward Pricing Pressure / GUPPI diversion-and-margin screen.
economic_models_vocabulary.entry_repositioning_analysis: Whether entry/repositioning is timely, likely, sufficient.
economic_models_vocabulary.failing_firm_defense: Failing/weakened-firm defense (imminent exit, no better buyer).
economic_models_vocabulary.divestiture_remedy_sufficiency: Whether a divestiture/fix-it restores lost competition.
economic_models_vocabulary.behavioral_remedy_firewall: Conduct/firewall commitments as a remedy or incentive constraint.
economic_models_vocabulary.buyer_power_customer_alternatives: Sophisticated buyers / alternative sources discipline price.
economic_models_vocabulary.nash_bargaining_vertical: Nash-bargaining vertical leverage / bargaining-model price effects.
economic_models_vocabulary.raising_rivals_costs: Conduct/integration that raises rivals' input or distribution costs.
economic_models_vocabulary.vertical_ability_incentive_foreclosure: Vertical foreclosure via ability + incentive (incl. data access).
economic_models_vocabulary.two_sided_platform_market: Single relevant market spanning both sides of a transaction platform.
economic_models_vocabulary.net_two_sided_price_test: Requirement to prove net harm across both platform sides.
economic_models_vocabulary.exclusive_dealing_foreclosure: Exclusive contracts foreclosing rivals from customers/inputs.
economic_models_vocabulary.distribution_channel_foreclosure: Foreclosure of the efficient distribution channel.
economic_models_vocabulary.scale_barrier_foreclosure: Returns-to-scale / data-scale barrier reinforced by conduct.
economic_models_vocabulary.monopsony_input_market: Buyer-side (input/labor) market power depressing input prices.
economic_models_vocabulary.bidding_auction_competition: Direct head-to-head bidding/auction rivalry as evidence.
economic_models_vocabulary.horizontal_restraint_effects: Rule-of-reason competitive-effects of a horizontal restraint/JV.
economic_models_vocabulary.mfn_facilitating_device: Most-favored-nation clause as a collusion-facilitating device.
economic_models_vocabulary.but_for_counterfactual: Liability but-for world (what competition would look like absent conduct).
economic_models_vocabulary.but_for_price_effects: Observed before/after price effects tied to the conduct.
economic_models_vocabulary.but_for_damages_model: Damages model quantifying the but-for overcharge.
economic_models_vocabulary.output_innovation_effects: Harm measured in reduced output/innovation, not just price.
economic_models_vocabulary.market_power_from_durable_share: Market power inferred from durable share + price stability.

field_notes.citation: { cite, stands_for:[{argument, disposition}] } — disposition is how the COURT treated that argument: 'approved' (accepted), 'rejected', 'mixed', or 'pending'.

cases.name: U.S. v. Microsoft Corp.

citation.cite: United States v. Microsoft Corp., 253 F.3d 34 (D.C. Cir. 2001); findings of fact, 84 F. Supp. 2d 9 (D.D.C. 1999)

stands_for.argument: Monopoly power may be inferred from durable dominant share plus a structural entry barrier (applications barrier), not only direct price evidence
A course of exclusionary conduct protecting an OS monopoly against middleware violates §2
Tying of IE to Windows is per se unlawful
Structural breakup is the appropriate remedy

cases.market: Intel-compatible PC operating systems
cases.theory_of_harm: Monopoly maintenance: exclusionary conduct against Netscape Navigator and Java ('middleware') that could erode the applications barrier to entry protecting the Windows OS monopoly.
cases.outcome_detail: D.C. Cir. (2001) affirmed §2 monopoly-maintenance liability, reversed the §1 tying holding and the breakup remedy, and remanded; settled 2001-2002.
winning_arguments: Monopoly power inferred from durable ~95% share plus the applications barrier to entry
A pattern of exclusionary acts (OEM/ISV/IAP restrictions, commingling code) that made sense only to protect the monopoly
Harm to nascent competition (middleware) counts even without proof it would certainly have succeeded
winning_evidence: internal documents showing intent to blunt the middleware threat
restrictive OEM/ISV/IAP contract terms
durable ~95% share + entry-barrier evidence
cases.judge_treatment: Court (and D.C. Cir.) accepted structural/barrier evidence of monopoly power over Schmalensee's price-based rebuttal, and judged the conduct as an aggregate course of action rather than crediting each act's standalone justification.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defense framed each act as independently procompetitive; court aggregated the course of conduct and found no valid justification net of exclusion.
cases.useful_for: Monopoly-maintenance / exclusionary conduct, platform defaults, nascent-competitor foreclosure, tech §2.

cases.name: U.S. v. Visa U.S.A., Inc. & MasterCard

citation.cite: United States v. Visa U.S.A., Inc., 163 F. Supp. 2d 322 (S.D.N.Y. 2001), aff'd, 344 F.3d 229 (2d Cir. 2003)

stands_for.argument: Rules barring member banks from issuing Amex/Discover foreclose rival networks and reduce output/innovation
Dual governance (banks on both networks) independently harms competition

cases.market: general-purpose card network services / issuing
cases.theory_of_harm: Exclusionary rules barred member banks from also issuing American Express or Discover, foreclosing rival networks and suppressing innovation; plus a rejected dual-governance claim.
cases.outcome_detail: Court (2001) struck the exclusionary rules; rejected the dual-governance claim. 2d Cir. affirmed (2003).
winning_arguments: Exclusionary rules foreclosed Amex/Discover from the largest distribution channel (member banks) and reduced network output/innovation
Harm to interbrand network competition, not just intrabrand
winning_evidence: the exclusionary bylaws themselves + bank-foreclosure data
evidence rival networks were kept out of the bank issuing channel
reduced-output/innovation evidence
cases.judge_treatment: Court credited the government's foreclosure and innovation-harm showing on the exclusionary rules but was unpersuaded that dual governance caused cognizable harm.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defense efficiency/cohesion justifications for exclusivity not credited against foreclosure of rival networks.
cases.useful_for: Exclusive-dealing / distribution foreclosure, network & platform competition, rules blocking multi-homing.

cases.name: U.S. v. Dentsply International, Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. Dentsply Int'l, Inc., 399 F.3d 181 (3d Cir. 2005); rev'g 277 F. Supp. 2d 387 (D. Del. 2003)

stands_for.argument: Barring dealers from carrying rivals unlawfully forecloses the efficient distribution channel even if direct sales are theoretically possible
The theoretical availability of a direct-sales channel defeats the foreclosure claim
Durable high share + price stability evidences market power and effective foreclosure

cases.market: prefabricated artificial teeth (U.S.)
cases.theory_of_harm: Dominant maker used dealer exclusivity ('Dealer Criterion 6') to bar distributors from carrying rivals' teeth, foreclosing the key channel and entrenching monopoly.
cases.outcome_detail: District court ruled for Dentsply; 3d Cir. reversed (2005), finding unlawful exclusive dealing.
winning_arguments: Dealers were the economically efficient gateway; foreclosing them raised rivals' costs even though direct sales were theoretically possible
Durable high prices/stable share evidenced market power and effective foreclosure
winning_evidence: Dealer Criterion 6 terms
years of durable share and price stability
evidence that dealer access was the efficient route to dentists/labs
cases.judge_treatment: Trial court accepted the 'rivals can sell direct' defense; 3d Cir. rejected it, treating dealer access as economically decisive and inferring foreclosure from durable share/price stability.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: The 'alternative channel exists' defense failed — the alternative was not a realistic competitive substitute.
cases.useful_for: Exclusive-dealing / distribution foreclosure, raising-rivals'-costs, 'alternative channel' rebuttals.

cases.name: U.S. v. Oracle Corp.

citation.cite: United States v. Oracle Corp., 331 F. Supp. 2d 1098 (N.D. Cal. 2004)

stands_for.argument: A narrow 'high-function' HRM/FMS relevant market excludes mid-market vendors, incumbents and outsourcing
Localized-competition unilateral-effects theory establishes likely harm
Wide competitive alternatives constrain post-merger pricing (defense)

cases.market: alleged high-function HR management (HRM) and financial management (FMS) software
cases.theory_of_harm: Merger to 3-to-2 (Oracle/PeopleSoft/SAP) in high-function ERP would enable unilateral price effects and localized coordinated effects.
cases.outcome_detail: Court ruled for defendants (Sept 2004): government failed to prove the narrow 'high-function' market or unilateral/coordinated effects.
winning_arguments: Government's product market was gerrymandered — mid-market vendors, incumbents, best-of-breed, outsourcing constrained pricing
Localized-competition/unilateral-effects theory unsupported by transaction evidence
winning_evidence: breadth-of-competition evidence (mid-market, incumbents, outsourcing)
customer/transaction testimony undercutting the narrow market and the strategic-pricing story
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Walker sharply criticized the localized-competition/unilateral-effects theory as economically and evidentiarily unsupported and rejected the narrow relevant market.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: DOJ's narrow market definition and unilateral-effects proof did not meet the burden.
cases.useful_for: Defending a merger via market definition; attacking a narrow market; unilateral-effects proof standards.

cases.name: U.S. v. American Express Co. (Ohio v. American Express)

citation.cite: Ohio v. American Express Co., 138 S. Ct. 2274 (2018); rev'g 88 F. Supp. 3d 143 (E.D.N.Y. 2015)

stands_for.argument: A two-sided transaction platform must be defined as a single market spanning both sides
Higher merchant fees alone establish anticompetitive harm
Plaintiff must prove a net price increase across both platform sides

cases.market: credit-card transactions (two-sided transaction platform)
cases.theory_of_harm: Amex's anti-steering rules barred merchants from steering to cheaper cards, keeping merchant fees high and suppressing interbrand price competition.
cases.outcome_detail: District court found for plaintiffs (2015); 2d Cir. reversed; SCOTUS (2018, 5-4) affirmed for Amex.
winning_arguments: A two-sided transaction platform is a single market spanning merchants and cardholders
Higher merchant fees alone are not harm — must prove net price increase across both sides
winning_evidence: evidence of cardholder-side benefits (rewards) offsetting merchant fees
two-sided output growth in the card industry
cases.judge_treatment: Trial court credited merchant-side price-effects proof; SCOTUS (Thomas, J.) rejected that framing, held the two sides are one market, and required net two-sided harm the plaintiffs never supplied.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Plaintiffs proved merchant-side harm but not two-sided net harm; the burden-shifting framework defeated the prima facie case.
cases.useful_for: Two-sided / platform markets, anti-steering & MFN rules, cases where a defendant invokes Amex to widen the market.

cases.name: U.S. v. H&R Block, Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. H&R Block, Inc., 833 F. Supp. 2d 36 (D.D.C. 2011)

stands_for.argument: Digital DIY tax prep is a distinct market; free/manual filing does not discipline paid DDIY pricing
Loss of TaxACT as a low-price maverick plus 3-to-2 concentration shows likely harm (unilateral + coordinated)
Entry/expansion would be timely, likely and sufficient (defense)

cases.market: digital do-it-yourself (DDIY) tax preparation products
cases.theory_of_harm: 3-to-2 among DDIY providers (with Intuit) enabling unilateral price effects and coordination; TaxACT was a low-price maverick.
cases.outcome_detail: Court enjoined (Nov 2011) — an early modern litigated merger block; endorsed unilateral-effects economics and rejected a broad market including free/manual filing.
winning_arguments: DDIY is a distinct market; free/manual alternatives don't discipline paid DDIY pricing
Loss of TaxACT as a low-price maverick + coordination risk in a 3-to-2 market
Entry not timely, likely or sufficient
winning_evidence: merger-to-3-to-2 concentration
TaxACT maverick/low-price internal documents
UPP/diversion estimates
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Howell was among the first to expressly credit UPP/upward-pricing-pressure analysis and the loss of a maverick, rejecting the defense's broad 'free alternatives' market.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defense efficiencies and 'broad market' story unpersuasive; parties' documents showed head-to-head rivalry.
cases.useful_for: Merger challenges, maverick loss, unilateral & coordinated effects, defining a market against 'free' alternatives.

cases.name: U.S. v. Bazaarvoice, Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. Bazaarvoice, Inc., No. 13-cv-00133, 2014 WL 203966 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 8, 2014)

stands_for.argument: Parties' contemporaneous documents naming each other as closest competitor prove anticompetitive effect
A quantified price-increase estimate is required to prove §7 harm
Entry/repositioning would restore competition (defense)

cases.market: product ratings & reviews (R&R) platforms
cases.theory_of_harm: Completed acquisition of closest rival PowerReviews eliminated head-to-head competition, enabling unilateral effects; challenged post-consummation.
cases.outcome_detail: Court found the merger unlawful (Jan 2014) and ordered divestiture; credited the parties' own 'hot' documents over sophisticated economic defenses.
winning_arguments: Contemporaneous documents showed the firms viewed each other as primary competitors and the deal as eliminating competition
Entry/repositioning not timely, likely, sufficient
No quantified price increase required where effect otherwise proven
winning_evidence: parties' ordinary-course 'hot' documents naming each other as closest competitor
deal-rationale documents describing eliminating a competitor
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Orrick gave decisive weight to the merging parties' strategic documents and discounted the defense economists, holding a quantified price-increase estimate is not required.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defense economic testimony couldn't overcome the parties' own damning documents.
cases.useful_for: Consummated-merger challenges, power of 'hot docs', closest-competitor unilateral effects, entry rebuttals.

cases.name: U.S. v. Apple, Inc. (E-books)

citation.cite: United States v. Apple, Inc., 952 F. Supp. 2d 638 (S.D.N.Y. 2013), aff'd, 791 F.3d 290 (2d Cir. 2015)

stands_for.argument: A vertical player can be liable as the 'hub' that organizes a horizontal price-fixing conspiracy
Simultaneous agency switch + MFNs facilitated and caused higher prices
Entering to compete with Amazon is a lawful procompetitive justification

cases.market: trade e-books
cases.theory_of_harm: Apple orchestrated a hub-and-spoke conspiracy with five publishers to switch to agency + MFNs, collectively raising e-book prices to undercut Amazon's $9.99.
cases.outcome_detail: Court found Apple liable (July 2013); 2d Cir. affirmed (2015).
winning_arguments: Apple was the hub enabling a horizontal price-fixing agreement
Agency + MFN across publishers predictably and actually raised prices
Vertical form doesn't immunize a scheme facilitating horizontal collusion
winning_evidence: communications/meeting evidence of publisher coordination via Apple
the simultaneous agency switch + MFN terms
post-switch price increases
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Cote credited the communications record and the observed post-agency price jump, treating the MFN and simultaneous switch as evidence of horizontal conspiracy rather than independent vertical dealing.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Apple's 'we entered to compete with Amazon' story couldn't overcome direct evidence of coordinating publisher pricing.
cases.useful_for: Hub-and-spoke / vertically-facilitated horizontal conspiracies, MFNs as facilitating devices, platform-entry defenses.

cases.name: U.S. v. AB Electrolux / General Electric (Appliances)

citation.cite: United States v. AB Electrolux, No. 1:15-cv-01039 (D.D.C. 2015) (deal abandoned mid-trial; no merits opinion)

stands_for.argument: 3-to-2 in contract-channel cooking appliances causes unilateral price effects

cases.market: major cooking appliances (ranges, cooktops, wall ovens) — contract/builder channel
cases.theory_of_harm: Electrolux acquiring GE appliances would create a 3-to-2, enabling unilateral price increases, especially in the contract channel.
cases.outcome_detail: During trial (Nov-Dec 2015) GE terminated the sale; DOJ effectively prevailed.
winning_arguments: Documents and win/loss data showed direct head-to-head rivalry, especially for builder/contract sales
Unilateral price effects in a concentrated cooking-appliance segment
winning_evidence: win/loss & builder-channel bidding data
party documents (introduced before the deal collapsed)
cases.judge_treatment: No merits opinion — the deal collapsed mid-trial after the government's head-to-head/bidding evidence came in; treatment inferred from abandonment.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Trial evidence of head-to-head competition undercut the efficiencies/broad-market defense before a ruling.
cases.useful_for: 3-to-2 mergers, contract/bidding-channel unilateral effects, deals that collapse mid-trial.

cases.name: U.S. v. Anthem, Inc. / Cigna Corp.

citation.cite: United States v. Anthem, Inc., 236 F. Supp. 3d 171 (D.D.C.), aff'd, 855 F.3d 345 (D.C. Cir. 2017)

stands_for.argument: National accounts (large multistate employers) is a distinct market where only a few insurers compete
Claimed medical-cost 'efficiencies' offset the merger's harm
Efficiencies must be merger-specific, verifiable and passed through (and cannot rest on monopsony)

cases.market: commercial health insurance for national accounts (large multistate employers); local group markets
cases.theory_of_harm: Merger of two 'Big Five' insurers would reduce competition for large national-account employers and in local markets.
cases.outcome_detail: Court enjoined (Feb 2017); D.C. Cir. affirmed (2017). Efficiencies rejected as not merger-specific/verifiable; the parties' own infighting undercut the deal rationale.
winning_arguments: National accounts is a distinct market; 4-to-3 harms large employers
Efficiencies fail: not merger-specific, verifiable, or passed through, and partly monopsony
Even the merging parties disagreed the deal would deliver claimed benefits
winning_evidence: national-accounts competition evidence
parties' own conflicting statements on the efficiencies
record showing the claimed savings weren't verifiable/passed-through
cases.judge_treatment: Court applied a demanding efficiencies standard and found the defense's medical-cost-savings model failed all three prongs; declined to credit savings stemming from buyer power.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defendants' efficiencies case was speculative and internally contradicted.
cases.useful_for: Merger efficiencies defenses (and how they fail), insurance, national vs local market definition.

cases.name: U.S. v. Aetna Inc. / Humana Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. Aetna Inc., 240 F. Supp. 3d 1 (D.D.C. 2017)

stands_for.argument: Medicare Advantage is a distinct market not disciplined by traditional Medicare
The proposed Molina divestiture restores lost competition
The defendants' ACA-exchange exit was a genuine business decision (not litigation-driven)

cases.market: individual Medicare Advantage (county-level); public exchanges (certain counties)
cases.theory_of_harm: Aetna/Humana would reduce MA competition in hundreds of counties and on ACA exchanges; a Molina divestiture was inadequate.
economic_methods: market definition (MA distinct from traditional Medicare)
cases.outcome_detail: Court enjoined (Jan 2017): MA is a separate market; the Molina divestiture wouldn't restore competition; exchange withdrawal was found litigation-driven.
winning_arguments: MA competes on its own terms, not disciplined by traditional Medicare
The divestiture buyer (Molina) couldn't replicate lost competition
Defendants' exchange exit was to manufacture a litigation position
winning_evidence: MA-specific competition & switching evidence
record showing Molina couldn't replace the competition
internal documents that the exchange exit was strategic
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Bates accepted the demand-substitution evidence that MA is a distinct market, rejected the Molina divestiture as insufficient, and found the exchange-exit evidence litigation-driven and not credible.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Market-definition and remedy both failed; the 'we already exited exchanges' argument backfired.
cases.useful_for: Merger market definition, divestiture/fix-it sufficiency, insurance, 'self-help' exit arguments.

cases.name: U.S. v. EnergySolutions, Inc. / Waste Control Specialists

citation.cite: United States v. Energy Solutions, Inc., 265 F. Supp. 3d 415 (D. Del. 2017)

stands_for.argument: Direct evidence of head-to-head bidding rivalry proves a merger to monopoly (no need for structural abstractions)
The failing/weakened-firm defense excuses the merger given WCS's losses

cases.market: disposal of low-level radioactive waste (LLRW) for commercial customers (certain regions)
cases.theory_of_harm: Merger of the only two significant LLRW disposal competitors would create a monopoly; parties raised a failing-firm defense for WCS.
cases.outcome_detail: Court enjoined (June 2017): direct evidence of head-to-head bidding; failing-firm defense rejected despite WCS losses.
winning_arguments: Direct evidence: the two firms bid against each other and lowered prices — a merger to monopoly
Failing-firm defense fails without imminent exit and no less-anticompetitive buyer
Financial losses ≠ competitive irrelevance
winning_evidence: direct head-to-head bidding records showing price competition
insufficient proof of imminent exit / no alternative buyer
cases.judge_treatment: Court relied on direct bidding-rivalry evidence over structural abstractions and held the failing-firm defense to its strict elements.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: The failing/weakened-firm defense didn't meet its elements; bidding data showed real rivalry.
cases.useful_for: Merger-to-monopoly, failing-firm/weakened-competitor defenses, bidding-market direct evidence.

cases.name: U.S. v. AT&T Inc. / DirecTV / Time Warner Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. AT&T, Inc., 310 F. Supp. 3d 161 (D.D.C. 2018), aff'd, 916 F.3d 1029 (D.C. Cir. 2019)

stands_for.argument: A Nash-bargaining vertical-leverage model proves the merger will raise rivals' programming costs and consumer prices
Real-world evidence (no price increases from comparable prior vertical deals; arbitration/no-blackout offer) rebuts the leverage theory
The vertical merger yields EDM efficiencies

cases.market: video programming (Turner content) + multichannel video distribution
cases.theory_of_harm: Vertical integration of distributor (AT&T/DirecTV) with must-have content (Turner) would raise rivals' costs and consumer prices via increased carriage bargaining leverage.
cases.outcome_detail: Court ruled for defendants (June 2018); D.C. Cir. affirmed (2019). The bargaining-leverage model was found unpersuasive against real-world evidence.
winning_arguments: Real-world evidence (no post-integration price increases from comparable deals) rebutted the theoretical model
Model assumptions shaky; Turner's irrevocable arbitration/no-blackout offer blunted foreclosure
Vertical mergers generate EDM efficiencies
winning_evidence: real-world benchmarks: no price increases from prior comparable vertical integrations
Turner's irrevocable arbitration / no-blackout commitment
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Leon gave little weight to Prof. Shapiro's Nash-bargaining model, calling it unpersuasive against real-world evidence, and credited the arbitration/no-blackout offer and EDM; the D.C. Cir. affirmed the factual rejection.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: The economic bargaining model wasn't corroborated by market facts; the court found it speculative.
cases.useful_for: Vertical mergers, bargaining-leverage models & their vulnerabilities, EDM, rebutting models with real-world evidence.

cases.name: U.S. v. CVS Health Corp. / Aetna Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. CVS Health Corp., 407 F. Supp. 3d 45 (D.D.C. 2019) (Tunney Act)

stands_for.argument: The Part D PDP horizontal overlap is cured by the divestiture to WellCare
Under the Tunney Act the decree is within the reaches of the public interest
Broader vertical PBM/insurer harms warrant rejecting the decree

cases.market: individual Medicare Part D prescription drug plans (horizontal overlap); vertical PBM/insurer concerns (amici)
cases.theory_of_harm: Horizontal overlap in individual Part D PDPs (remedied by divestiture); amici argued broader vertical foreclosure from combining a large insurer with a PBM and retail pharmacy.
cases.posture: consent decree + contested Tunney Act evidentiary hearing
cases.outcome_detail: DOJ settled with divestiture of Aetna's Part D PDP business (to WellCare); after a live-witness Tunney Act hearing, Judge Leon approved the final judgment (Sept 2019).
winning_arguments: The narrow horizontal overlap (Part D PDPs) was cured by a clean divestiture
Under the Tunney Act the court's role is limited; the decree is in the public interest
winning_evidence: clean Part D divestiture to WellCare
limited Tunney Act record cabining the inquiry
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Leon held an unusual live-witness Tunney Act hearing and voiced process skepticism but ultimately deferred, treating amici's broader vertical economics as beyond the limited 'public interest' inquiry.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Amici's broader vertical-harm theories were outside the scope for rejecting a §7 settlement.
cases.useful_for: Vertical mergers with settlements, Tunney Act practice, divestiture remedies, scope of decree review.

cases.name: U.S. v. Sabre Corp. / Farelogix Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. Sabre Corp., 452 F. Supp. 3d 97 (D. Del. 2020) (later vacated as moot after the deal was abandoned)

stands_for.argument: Under Amex, a two-sided transaction platform (Sabre) and a one-sided input supplier (Farelogix) are not in one relevant market and do not compete
The merger eliminates a disruptive innovator, causing competitive harm

cases.market: booking/distribution technology serving airlines and travel agencies (GDS vs. direct-connect)
cases.theory_of_harm: Sabre (dominant GDS) acquiring innovative Farelogix would eliminate a disruptive rival and entrench Sabre.
cases.outcome_detail: Court ruled for defendants (Apr 2020): applying Amex, Sabre is a two-sided transaction platform serving airlines and agencies while Farelogix does not serve agencies in the same market. DOJ appealed; mooted after the UK CMA blocked the deal.
winning_arguments: Amex two-sided framing: Sabre spans airlines and agencies; Farelogix does not, so no single shared relevant market
Government's effects proof depended on a market the court rejected
winning_evidence: evidence of the two-sided transaction structure of Sabre vs. one-sided Farelogix
product-usage evidence that Farelogix didn't serve travel agencies
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Stark applied Ohio v. Amex to a two-sided transaction platform and held the firms did not compete in one market, neutralizing the government's diversion/effects economics regardless of merit.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: The court's application of Amex defeated the government's market definition.
cases.useful_for: Two-sided platform market definition, innovation-loss theories, Amex as a merger defense, tech/distribution deals.
cases.note: This case appears in two folders in the database — consider de-duplicating.

cases.name: U.S. and Plaintiff States v. Google LLC (Search)

citation.cite: United States v. Google LLC, No. 1:20-cv-03010 (D.D.C. Aug. 5, 2024) (liability op.) (reported at 747 F. Supp. 3d 1 — verify pinpoint)

stands_for.argument: Exclusive default-placement agreements foreclosed rivals from query scale and unlawfully maintained a search monopoly
Scale/query volume is a barrier to entry that conduct reinforced
Google's dominance reflects only a superior product and easy user switching (defense)

cases.market: general search services; general search text advertising
cases.theory_of_harm: Google maintained its search monopoly through exclusive default-placement agreements (Apple, Android OEMs/carriers, browsers) that foreclosed rivals from the scale needed to compete.
cases.outcome_detail: Court held (Aug 2024) that 'Google is a monopolist' and unlawfully maintained monopoly via exclusive distribution agreements; remedies followed.
winning_arguments: Default placement is decisive; paying billions for exclusivity foreclosed rivals from query scale
Scale is a barrier — rivals can't match quality without the volume they were denied
Conduct, not just a superior product, explains durable dominance
winning_evidence: the default-agreement contracts + sums paid for exclusivity
internal analyses of default power and switching inertia
scale/query-volume evidence
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Mehta credited Prof. Whinston's foreclosure-and-scale account over Prof. Murphy's 'competition is a click away' rebuttal, finding the exclusive defaults, not merely quality, sustained the monopoly.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defense 'we win on quality / users can switch' story couldn't overcome the exclusivity + scale-foreclosure evidence.
cases.useful_for: Platform §2 monopoly-maintenance, exclusive defaults/distribution, scale-and-data barriers, remedies design.

cases.name: U.S. and Plaintiff States v. American Airlines / JetBlue (Northeast Alliance)

citation.cite: United States v. American Airlines Grp. Inc., No. 1:21-cv-11558 (D. Mass. May 19, 2023) (findings of fact & conclusions of law)

stands_for.argument: A broad revenue-sharing JV that removes the incentive to compete on overlapping routes is an unreasonable restraint (a de facto merger there)
The NEA's claimed consumer benefits justify the restraint under the rule of reason

cases.market: scheduled air passenger service on Boston/New York-area routes
cases.theory_of_harm: The NEA — a broad revenue-sharing JV between American and JetBlue — eliminated head-to-head competition in the Northeast, a de facto merger there.
economic_methods: loss of JetBlue as a disruptor
cases.outcome_detail: Court ruled for plaintiffs (May 2023) and ordered the NEA unwound; JetBlue did not appeal (American did).
winning_arguments: The NEA removed the incentive to compete on overlapping routes — the anticompetitive core outweighed the benefits
JetBlue's role as a low-fare disruptor was neutralized
Efficiency justifications not sufficient under the rule of reason
winning_evidence: capacity/output data on overlap routes
internal NEA planning documents
evidence JetBlue lost its independent competitive incentive
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Sorokin credited the plaintiffs' loss-of-rivalry and output-effects evidence and found the claimed consumer benefits neither sufficiently proven nor achievable only via so broad a restraint.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: The pro-competitive JV benefits didn't outweigh the elimination of rivalry between two significant competitors.
cases.useful_for: Airline/JV restraints, rule-of-reason JVs, 'de facto merger' coordination, disruptor-loss theories.

cases.name: U.S. v. Bertelsmann SE (Penguin Random House / Simon & Schuster)

citation.cite: United States v. Bertelsmann SE & Co. KGaA, 646 F. Supp. 3d 1 (D.D.C. 2022)

stands_for.argument: A buyer-side 'anticipated top-sellers' input market (advances ≥ ~$250k) is a valid relevant market
The merger would lessen competition and depress author advances (monopsony harm)
Claimed efficiencies and 'imprints will keep bidding against each other' rebut the harm

cases.market: U.S. publishing rights to anticipated top-selling books (advances ≥ ~$250k) — a buyer-side (monopsony) input market
cases.theory_of_harm: PRH acquiring Simon & Schuster would concentrate the buy side for high-advance book rights, depressing author advances.
cases.outcome_detail: Court enjoined the merger (Oct/Nov 2022) on a monopsony theory — a landmark labor/input-side merger challenge.
winning_arguments: Antitrust protects the buy side: fewer bidders for top titles means lower advances
The 'anticipated top-sellers' input market is valid with head-to-head bidding
Efficiencies and internal-competition promises were speculative/unenforceable
winning_evidence: bidding/auction records for top titles
concentration on high advances
internal deal documents
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Pan credited DOJ expert Nicholas Hill's input-market concentration and bidding analysis and rejected defense expert Edward Snyder's efficiencies and 'imprints will still bid' rebuttal as speculative/unenforceable.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defense efficiencies (Snyder) and 'imprints still compete' claims didn't rebut the monopsony effects on advances.
cases.useful_for: Monopsony / buy-side mergers, labor & input-market theories, bidding markets, efficiencies rebuttal.

cases.name: U.S. v. United States Sugar Corp. (Imperial Sugar)

citation.cite: United States v. U.S. Sugar Corp., 636 F. Supp. 3d 468 (D. Del. 2022), aff'd, 73 F.4th 197 (3d Cir. 2023)

stands_for.argument: A separate refined-sugar 'distribution' relevant market exists
Sophisticated customers with alternative sources / buyer power constrain post-merger pricing (defense)
The government's competitive-effects model proves harm

cases.market: alleged sale/distribution of refined sugar to customers in the Southeastern U.S.
cases.theory_of_harm: U.S. Sugar acquiring Imperial Sugar would reduce competition and raise prices for Southeastern refined-sugar customers.
cases.outcome_detail: Court ruled for defendants (Sept 2022); 3d Cir. affirmed (2023). The distribution-market definition was rejected — customers had adequate alternative sources.
winning_arguments: No separate 'distribution' market — producers and other suppliers constrained pricing
Large industrial customers had credible alternatives and buyer power
The government's expert model rested on the flawed market
winning_evidence: customer-alternative & buyer-power evidence
record undercutting a distribution-only market
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Williams found DOJ expert Dov Rothman's competitive-effects analysis unpersuasive because it depended on a distribution-level market the court rejected; the 3d Cir. affirmed.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: DOJ's relevant-market theory failed on customer alternatives and buyer sophistication.
cases.useful_for: Merger market definition, distribution-level markets, buyer-power/customer-alternative defenses, commodities.

cases.name: U.S. v. UnitedHealth Group Inc. / Change Healthcare Inc.

citation.cite: United States v. UnitedHealth Grp. Inc., 630 F. Supp. 3d 118 (D.D.C. 2022)

stands_for.argument: The merged firm would have the ability to foreclose rivals via access to their claims data
The merged firm would have the incentive to misuse that data / foreclose
Firewall commitments + the ClaimsXten divestiture resolve the concerns

cases.market: vertical: insurer/Optum + Change (claims clearinghouse / EDI, first-pass claims editing); horizontal overlap in first-pass editing
cases.theory_of_harm: UnitedHealth (Optum) acquiring Change would give access to rivals' sensitive claims data and the ability/incentive to foreclose competing insurers; plus a horizontal overlap.
economic_methods: vertical foreclosure / access to rival data
cases.outcome_detail: Court ruled for defendants (Sept 2022): credited firewall commitments and the ClaimsXten divestiture (to TPG); found no proven incentive to misuse data and no horizontal harm.
winning_arguments: No proven incentive to foreclose — reputational/contractual constraints made misuse unlikely; firewall credited
The divestiture cured the horizontal overlap
Vertical foreclosure theory too speculative
winning_evidence: firewall commitments + ClaimsXten divestiture
reputational/contractual-constraint evidence negating incentive to foreclose
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Nichols accepted the ability prong but found the government failed the incentive prong, discounting Prof. Gowrisankaran's foreclosure model in favor of the firewall commitments and reputational-constraint evidence; credited the divestiture on the horizontal claim.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: DOJ couldn't establish incentive (not just ability) to foreclose, and behavioral/structural remedies were accepted.
cases.useful_for: Vertical mergers, data-foreclosure theories, ability-vs-incentive, behavioral remedies/firewalls, divestiture fixes.

cases.name: U.S. v. Booz Allen Hamilton / EverWatch

citation.cite: United States v. Booz Allen Hamilton Inc., No. 1:22-cv-01603 (D. Md. Oct. 31, 2022)

stands_for.argument: Eliminating the only two expected bidders for a single NSA procurement substantially lessens competition
The contracting agency retained tools to restructure/re-compete and preserve competition (defense)

cases.market: operational modeling & simulation services for a specific NSA SIGINT procurement (OPTIMAL MIND)
cases.theory_of_harm: Booz Allen acquiring EverWatch would eliminate the only two expected competitors for a single government contract.
cases.outcome_detail: Court ruled for defendants (Oct 2022): DOJ did not show a likely substantial lessening of competition for the procurement; deal closed.
winning_arguments: The government could restructure/re-compete the procurement; the agency retained tools to preserve competition
No sufficiently probable, cognizable lessening of competition for the single contract
winning_evidence: evidence the contracting agency could restructure or re-compete the procurement
cases.judge_treatment: The court found the single-procurement bidding theory did not establish a sufficiently probable substantial lessening of competition, emphasizing the agency's own tools to preserve competition.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: The narrow single-procurement theory didn't carry the §7/§1 burden on likely harm.
cases.useful_for: Government-contracting/bidding mergers, single-procurement markets, competition-for-the-contract theories.

cases.name: U.S. v. ASSA ABLOY AB / Spectrum Brands (HHI)

citation.cite: United States v. ASSA ABLOY AB, No. 1:22-cv-03290 (D.D.C. 2022) (resolved by consent decree with divestiture; no merits opinion)

stands_for.argument: Premium residential door hardware / smart locks is a distinct segment where the deal lost a close competitor
A structural divestiture is required to preserve competition

cases.market: premium mechanical door hardware and smart locks (residential)
cases.theory_of_harm: ASSA ABLOY acquiring Spectrum's HHI would reduce competition in premium residential door hardware and smart locks.
cases.outcome_detail: After the DOJ trial began, the parties agreed to a consent decree divesting the relevant hardware businesses (to Fortune Brands).
winning_arguments: Premium door hardware / smart locks is a distinct segment; the deal was 3-to-2 / lost a close competitor
A structural divestiture was required
winning_evidence: premium-segment closeness & concentration evidence that led to a divestiture settlement
cases.judge_treatment: No merits opinion — the case settled during trial with a structural divestiture; treatment inferred from the government-favorable resolution.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Facing the unilateral-effects case, defendants divested rather than litigate to judgment.
cases.useful_for: Consumer-durables mergers, premium-segment market definition, unilateral effects, litigate-then-settle-with-divestiture.

cases.name: U.S. and Plaintiff States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech)

citation.cite: United States v. Google LLC, No. 1:23-cv-00108 (E.D. Va. Apr. 17, 2025) (liability op.)

stands_for.argument: Publisher ad servers and ad exchanges are distinct relevant markets that Google unlawfully monopolized and tied
The advertiser ad-network market claim is proven

cases.market: publisher ad servers; ad exchanges; advertiser ad networks (open-web display)
cases.theory_of_harm: Google monopolized and tied the ad-tech stack (publisher ad server + ad exchange), entrenching dominance across the open-web display pipeline.
cases.outcome_detail: Court found (Apr 2025) Google unlawfully monopolized/tied in two of three markets (publisher ad servers, ad exchanges); found for Google on the advertiser-network market.
winning_arguments: Distinct ad-tech tool markets exist; the server and exchange are separate products unlawfully tied
Conduct (auction rules, integration) foreclosed rivals and entrenched dominance
winning_evidence: auction-rule & product-integration conduct evidence
distinct-tool usage evidence for ad server & exchange
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Brinkema accepted the plaintiffs' distinct-tool market definitions and tying/foreclosure economics for ad servers and exchanges but found the market/effects proof insufficient for the advertiser-network market.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Google prevailed on the advertiser-network market where the plaintiffs' market definition/effects proof fell short.
cases.useful_for: Ad-tech / platform §2, tying across a technology stack, multi-market monopolization, digital-tool market definition.

cases.name: U.S. and Plaintiff States v. JetBlue Airways / Spirit Airlines

citation.cite: United States v. JetBlue Airways Corp., No. 1:23-cv-10511 (D. Mass. Jan. 16, 2024) (reported at 712 F. Supp. 3d 109 — verify pinpoint)

stands_for.argument: Removing Spirit's ultra-low-cost fares harms price-sensitive travelers on overlapping routes
Claimed capacity/consumer efficiencies offset the harm

cases.market: scheduled air passenger service (numerous route overlaps); ultra-low-cost / price-sensitive segment
cases.theory_of_harm: JetBlue acquiring Spirit — the largest ULCC — would remove Spirit's disruptive low fares, harming price-sensitive travelers.
cases.outcome_detail: Court enjoined the merger (Jan 2024); JetBlue abandoned the deal. Loss of Spirit's ULCC competition outweighed the claimed benefits; efficiencies rejected.
winning_arguments: Spirit's ultra-low fares uniquely discipline pricing for cost-conscious flyers; the merger removes that
Claimed benefits not merger-specific/verifiable and don't offset harm to the price-sensitive segment
winning_evidence: route-overlap fare data showing Spirit's low-fare discipline
internal capacity-cut plans
unverifiable efficiencies
cases.judge_treatment: Judge Young emphasized the loss of Spirit's unique ULCC price discipline and rejected the defendants' claimed efficiencies as not merger-specific, verifiable, or sufficient.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Efficiency and 'more JetBlue competition vs. legacies' story didn't offset the ULCC-disruptor loss.
cases.useful_for: Airline mergers, disruptor/maverick loss, segment-specific harm (price-sensitive consumers), efficiencies defense.

cases.name: U.S. and Plaintiff States v. Live Nation Entertainment / Ticketmaster

citation.cite: United States v. Live Nation Entertainment, Inc., No. 1:24-cv-03973 (S.D.N.Y.) (pending — no merits opinion)

stands_for.argument: Exclusive venue ticketing contracts + tying of promotion and ticketing unlawfully maintain a ticketing monopoly

cases.market: primary concert ticketing; concert promotion; large-amphitheater / venue services
cases.theory_of_harm: Live Nation/Ticketmaster maintains a ticketing monopoly and forecloses rivals through exclusive venue contracts, tying/bundling promotion with ticketing, and amphitheater leverage.

key_experts.name: TBD (Daubert briefing referenced Hill, Anderson, Abrantes-Metz, Meyer)

cases.outcome_detail: Filed May 2024; ongoing as of the data snapshot. No merits judgment yet.
winning_arguments: (Alleged) exclusive multi-year venue ticketing contracts foreclose rival ticketers
(Alleged) leverage of promotion + amphitheater assets to protect ticketing dominance
winning_evidence: (alleged) exclusive venue contracts
(alleged) bundling of promotion + ticketing — not yet adjudicated
cases.judge_treatment: No merits ruling yet; Daubert motions to exclude expert testimony (Hill, Anderson, Abrantes-Metz, Meyer) are in the record — expert treatment still to be decided.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: n/a — pending; use for framing, not outcome precedent.
cases.useful_for: Live-entertainment / ticketing §2, exclusive venue contracts, tying + vertical leverage, ongoing-matter framing.

cases.name: Steves & Sons, Inc. v. JELD-WEN, Inc.

citation.cite: Steves & Sons, Inc. v. JELD-WEN, Inc., 988 F.3d 690 (4th Cir. 2021); district, 345 F. Supp. 3d 614 (E.D. Va. 2018)

stands_for.argument: A prior consummated acquisition harmed a captive input (doorskins) market on which independent doormakers depend
A private plaintiff facing threatened supply loss may obtain divestiture, not just damages

cases.market: interior molded doorskins (input) and molded doors
cases.theory_of_harm: JELD-WEN's earlier acquisition of CraftMaster (doorskins) let it foreclose/squeeze independent doormakers like Steves who depend on doorskins — a private §7 challenge seeking divestiture.
cases.outcome_detail: Jury found for Steves; district court ordered JELD-WEN to divest a doorskin plant — a rare private-plaintiff §7 divestiture; 4th Cir. largely affirmed (2021).
winning_arguments: The prior acquisition harmed a captive input market on which independent doormakers depended
Antitrust injury + threatened supply loss supported structural divestiture, not just damages
Post-merger price/quality/supply squeeze evidenced the effect
winning_evidence: evidence of a price/quality/supply squeeze on the captive doorskin input
Singer's foreclosure analysis
threatened supply-loss evidence supporting divestiture
cases.judge_treatment: The jury credited plaintiff expert Hal Singer's input-foreclosure and squeeze case; the district court and 4th Cir. accepted that a private plaintiff facing threatened supply loss could obtain divestiture, not just damages.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: Defendant's integration/efficiency story didn't overcome the input-foreclosure evidence.
cases.useful_for: Private §7 challenges, vertical input foreclosure, divestiture as a private remedy, captive-input markets.

cases.name: Duke Energy Carolinas v. NTE Carolinas II (and related claims)

citation.cite: Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC v. NTE Carolinas II, LLC, No. 3:19-cv-00515 (W.D.N.C.); see 4th Cir. 2020 (vacating preliminary injunction) — citation & final outcome UNVERIFIED

stands_for.argument: The incumbent used control of interconnection/transmission and targeted conduct to exclude a new generator (§2)

cases.market: wholesale electricity generation/supply in the Carolinas
cases.theory_of_harm: NTE, a new entrant generator, alleged Duke used exclusionary conduct (interconnection/transmission delays, targeted contracting, sham conduct) to monopolize wholesale power.
economic_methods: entry deterrence in regulated network industry
cases.posture: preliminary injunction + appeal (4th Cir. remand); further proceedings
cases.outcome_detail: 4th Cir. (2020) vacated a preliminary injunction and remanded; subsequent trial-court proceedings. FINAL OUTCOME NOT VERIFIED — check the folder docs before relying on it.
winning_arguments: (NTE) incumbent used control of interconnection/transmission to exclude a new generator
(Duke) legitimate business conduct / regulated-industry justifications
winning_evidence: interconnection/transmission conduct evidence — disposition unverified
cases.judge_treatment: UNVERIFIED — the 4th Cir. vacated an early preliminary injunction; how the fact-finder ultimately treated the economic/exclusionary-conduct evidence is not confirmed. Verify against the folder.

cases.name: Ninth Inning, Inc. v. National Football League (NFL Sunday Ticket)

citation.cite: In re NFL Sunday Ticket Antitrust Litig., 933 F.3d 1136 (9th Cir. 2019) (reversing dismissal); post-verdict JMOL vacating the jury award, No. 2:15-ml-02668 (C.D. Cal. 2024)

stands_for.argument: Pooling out-of-market telecasts into a single exclusive package can be an unreasonable output restriction (claim viable — dismissal reversed)
Plaintiffs' expert damages models (college-model and a-la-carte) reliably measure the but-for overcharge

cases.market: live telecasts of out-of-market professional (NFL) football games
cases.theory_of_harm: The NFL and teams pooled out-of-market telecast rights and sold them exclusively through one premium package (DirecTV 'Sunday Ticket'), restricting output and inflating prices vs. a competitive world.
cases.outcome: plaintiff jury verdict vacated by the court
cases.outcome_detail: 9th Cir. (2019) revived the case; a 2024 jury returned a multibillion-dollar verdict for the class, but the district court granted JMOL and vacated the verdict (2024), largely on the damages models. Appeal followed.
winning_arguments: (Plaintiffs, at trial) exclusive single-package distribution restricted output and raised prices
(Defendants, post-trial) the damages models weren't tied to a legally viable but-for world and were speculative/unreliable
winning_evidence: at trial: output-restriction & overcharge evidence (jury credited)
post-trial: damages models found unreliable on JMOL, verdict vacated
cases.judge_treatment: The jury credited plaintiffs' experts, but Judge Gutierrez granted JMOL and vacated the verdict, holding the Rascher and Zona damages models unreliable and untethered to a legally cognizable but-for world — a cautionary example of a court rejecting the experts' damages methodology post-verdict.
cases.why_the_loser_lost: The plaintiffs' expert damages models were found unreliable, leading the court to vacate the verdict.
cases.useful_for: Sports/broadcast output-restriction cases, exclusive-distribution §1, and the risk that a weak but-for/damages model sinks an otherwise-strong liability case.
